Agenda reports and other disclosable public records relating to each agenda item are available on the City's

MINUTES
  ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING
  MARCH 9, 2022

CHAIR STEGURA called the meeting of the Environmental Advisory Committee of the City of
Rolling Hills Estates to order at 7:05 p.m.

2.  ROLL CALL

COMMITTEE MEMBERS PRESENT:  Stegura, Bain, Chuang, Friedman, Low, Olson,
  O’Malley, Radocchio, Tarr, Uppal

COMMITTEE MEMBERS ABSENT:  Bacinski, Larson

STAFF MEMBERS PRESENT:  Alexa Davis, Assistant City Manager
  Jeannie Naughton, Planning Manager
  Carol Corea, Administrative Assistant

3.  APPROVAL OF MINUTES

A.  APPROVAL OF ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING, DECEMBER
  15, 2021

COMMITTEE MEMBER RADOCCHIO made a motion, seconded by COMMITTEE MEMBER
O’MALLEY to,

  APPROVE THE ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING MINUTES OF
  DECEMBER 15, 2021

There being no objection, CHAIR STEGURA so ordered.

4.  AUDIENCE ITEMS/ORAL COMMUNICATION ON ITEMS NOT ON THE AGENDA

NONE

5.  DISCUSSION ITEMS

A. CLEAN POWER ALLIANCE (CPA) NON-RESIDENTIAL DEFAULT RATE CHANGES

Planning Manager Naughton provided a presentation summarizing the staff report.

Staff reported that the City received input from the Palos Verdes Peninsula (PVP) Chamber of
Commerce, and they were supportive of providing the non-residential customers with an
education campaign to encourage to opt-up to 100% as opposed to defaulting them to that rate.

Planning Manager Naughton stated that the discussion item is whether or not to have the default
rate tier to remain at 50% or to opt-up to the 100% default rate tier for non-residential customers.
If a change is made, it would take effect in October of 2022.

Staff recommends that the Environmental Advisory Committee discuss the various options and
determine which renewable default rate tier would be most appropriate for Non-Residential
customers in the City of Rolling Hills Estates; and provide a recommendation to the City Council
regarding an appropriate default rate tier for non-residential customers

COMMITTEE MEMBER FRIEDMAN inquired about how the rate default works. Planning
Manager Naughton provided a brief explanation and stated that customers may opt down or up
at any time and once a customer makes changes to their tier then they are excluded from any
default changes.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BAIN inquired why CPA is adjusting its rates up to the SCE rates for the
100% tier. Planning Manager Naughton stated that when the CCA’s started, they had to be able
to compare the rates they were going to offer to the Investor-Owned Utility (IOU) so that customers
could have some kind of understanding of the difference in cost. All of the CCA’s in the state have
benchmarked their rates to IOU rates, at least initially, and this is a way to show the benefits
between the two programs. CHAIR STEGURA added that the theory was that renewable energy

 ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING
  1
 MINUTES, MARCH 9, 2022
 is becoming more available and SCE and other big providers are able to find more renewable
energy in the market as a whole. When CPA was attracting a base that wanted higher degrees of
renewable energy, that would force the utility companies, in a market sense, to buy cleaner
energy.

COMMITTEE MEMBER RADOCCHIO stated that he agreed with the PVP Chamber of
Commerce’s recommendation.

COMMITTEE MEMBER LOW inquired about the educational campaign and how it would work.
Planning Manager Naughton stated that in terms of noticing, the CPA provides two notices before
the change and two notices after the change, but aside from that, they do not provide additional
noticing. The City has until the end of the month to let CPA know if the default rate will be changed,
and there is not a lot of time to do independent outreach to the business community. An
“educational campaign” for businesses would be through social media, email blasts, and phone
calls; this would be the most cost-effective way to provide this information. The next CPA default
rate change could be made in two years.

COMMITTEE MEMBER RADOCCHIO made a motion, seconded by COMMITTEE MEMBER
LOW to,

  MAKE A RECOMMENDATION TO THE CITY COUNCIL THAT NON-RESIDENTIAL
  CUSTOMERS REMAIN AT THE 50% DEFAULT RATE TIER.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BAIN commented that since the policy of the City is to encourage 100%
green energy, then the commercial district should be defaulted to the policy of the City and then
if they want to make the change to a different tier, they can do so.

The Committee voted 6-3 approving the motion to recommend to the City Council that non-
residential customers remain at the 50% default rate tier.

CHAIR STEGURA stated that committee members are welcome to speak at the next regular City
Council meeting at which this item will be on the agenda.

B. ELECTRIC VEHICLE CHARGING STATION GRANT AWARD FOR CITY HALL
  INSTALLATION UPDATE (VERBAL REPORT)

Assistant City Manager Davis provided an update on the grant award for electric vehicle charging
stations for City Hall. The city had an opportunity to participate in SCE’s Charge Ready Program,
and the application was approved to install electrical vehicle charging stations at City Hall. The
city submitted an application for ten connections; however, SCE said they would do twelve
connections. A conceptual design was presented to the committee.

Assistant City Manager Davis stated that Highridge Park is not feasible for this program due to
the amount of infrastructure that would be needed. Separately, the city has received another grant
award that would provide support for charging stations at Ernie Howlett Park.

Assistant City Manager Davis thanked the committee for helping guide this project.

CHAIR STEGURA commended staff for procuring these grants.

C. SB 1383 ORGANICS WASTE IMPLEMENTATION UPDATE (VERBAL REPORT)

Assistant City Manager Davis provided a presentation with an update on SB 1383 – Mandatory
Organic Waste Recycling. The City has worked with Waste Management to implement some
measures and will be revising the City’s Municipal Code, which has helped to keep the City ahead
of the required implementation dates.

A list of the City’s responsibilities under the regulation was provided. The City submitted for a
grant through CalRecycle, and has heard that everyone who applied will receive the minimum
award amount. The grant will be utilized for consultant services who have expertise with this
regulation and for costs associated with development of the program. Starting January 1, 2024,
jurisdictions must demonstrate enforcement of these regulations.

Assistant City Manager Davis provided an overview of the City’s organic waste recycling program,
which began on July 1, 2021. In addition, an overview of the City’s future requirements was also
provided.

 CHAIR STEGURA asked if this information was provided to the HOAs. Assistant City Manager
Davis stated that this was done leading up to the launch and will reach out to the HOAs with more
information. The City’s website, www.rhe.city/waste, has information on waste and this program.

COMMITTEE MEMBER FRIEDMAN expressed the difficulty with the organic waste bin and stated
that a solution would be to provide a bag that fits in the bin that can be closed and placed into the
green bin. Assistant City Manager Davis stated that she has noticed the challenges as well and
is working with Waste Management to find a solution.

COMMITTEE MEMBER UPPAL commended the City for providing the containers and education
pamphlet because she has heard that other cities did not provide information to residents and
they had to come up with their own solution for food waste.

COMMITTEE MEMBER LOW made a suggestion to provide the pamphlet for this and any other
programs to the schools to include in children’s backpacks. This could be a way to get the word
out to parents in the community.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BAIN stated that there is an app called “Too Good To Go”, which allows
participating restaurants to provide meals at discounted prices typically at the end of the evening.

D. WATER SHORTAGE UPDATE (VERBAL UPDATE)

Planning Manager Naughton stated that over the year, there have been executive orders issued
in relation to the drought. The latest executive order called for statewide conservation measures
in October 2021. The State Water Resources Control Board adopted an emergency drought
conservation regulation that went into effect in January 2022. CalWater adopts a water shortage
contingency plan and within that plan are stages 1 through 6 of their water emergency response
plan. Rolling Hills Estates is in Stage 1. At this time, there is no need for the City to take further
action by moving into a stricter emergency plan.

Planning Manager Naughton stated that CalWater has started a program called the Water Loss
Auditing and Control Program, where they will come out to your business or residence to identify
any improvements that could be made to conserve water. In addition, and overview of the various
programs available by CalWater was also provided.

CHAIR STEGURA stated that CalWater is at the basic level now. If more stringent water saving
is needed, then this will come back to the EAC, and that time, the committee could recommend
to the City Council, that more stringent measures be put in place to save water.

E. TURF REPLACEMENT WATER USE INVENTORY AT CITY HALL UPDATE (VERBAL
  REPORT)

Assistant City Manager Davis stated that the City Council set a goal for water conservation for
City properties. As part of this, the City has worked with CalWater to identify areas that could help
conserve water. CalWater has identified a program that will provide over $200K to do turf
replacement for both Highridge Park and City Hall.

If the turf replacement is done at City Hall, the rebate will be $93K, which will require a
demonstration garden to be installed. For Highridge Park, the rebate will be approximately $144K.
There has been an increase in water rates resulting in increased costs to the City.

CHAIR STEGURA suggested working with the Palos Verdes Peninsula Land Conservancy for
the native plants and the demonstration garden. She also suggested that a tour be scheduled
with the EAC to walk both of the sites.

Assistant City Manager Davis stated that there was a suggestion to establish a subcommittee and
include members of the EAC, P&A Commission, and City Council.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BAIN inquired about a breakdown for the cost of the turf replacement at
Highridge Park. Assistant City Manager Davis stated that Highridge Park has a larger square
footage; CalWater will be in attendance at the next Park and Activities Commission meeting.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BAIN asked about Ernie Howlett Park. Assistant City Manager Davis
stated that it has not been reviewed for the rebate project; however, it is being looked at as far as
the infrastructure and usage, in order to identify any inefficiencies.

COMMITTEE MEMBER FRIEDMAN stated that the areas that are not fields are horse trails.
Assistant City Manager Davis stated that the City’s Maintenance Superintendent went out with

 ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING

 CalWater for the inspection and identified specific areas. There may be areas where there is
irrigation and it might be removed or improved to a higher efficiency level.

6.  MANAGER ITEMS

A. EARTH DAY PLANNING COMMITTEE AND VOLUNTEER OPPORTUNITIES

Assistant City Manager Davis stated that Earth Day will be in person on Friday April 22nd at the
Promenade Mall from 3pm to 6pm.

7.  COMMITTEE ITEMS/FUTURE AGENDA ITEMS

COMMITTEE MEMBER TARR provided future items, including looking into: 1) the concentration
of PM2.5 particulate matter, which may be impacting the City; 2) there is a chemical waste
disposal site in the Pacific Ocean off Palos Verdes Peninsula toward Catalina Island; 3) there is
a chemical compound known as PFAS, which are impacting drinking water in many cities in the
United States and the City needs to know whether or not their drinking water is being impacted.

8.  ADJOURNMENT

CHAIR STEGURA made a motion, seconded by COMMITTEE MEMBER UPPAL to,

  ADJOURN THE EAC MEETING AT 8:40 p.m.

There being no objection, CHAIR STEGURA so ordered.
